TRANSLATOR'S NOTE
 

Note that in the following translation the numbers 
without brackets refer to this text, while the numbers in square brackets refer

. 
These have been provided by the translator. Stage directions have also been

HISTORICAL NOTE

 

Aristophanes (c. 456 BC to c. 
386 BC) was the foremost writer of comic drama in classical Athens. His 
surviving plays are the only complete examples we have of Old Comedy. 

Frogs
 was 
first produced in Athens in 405 BC, where it won first prize in the competition. By this time Athens had been at war with 
Sparta for over twenty-five years.

 

 

DRAMATIS PERSONAE

 

XANTHIAS: a slave

DIONYSUS: the god, appearing in human form as a 
middle-aged man

HERCULES: the legendary hero

CORPSE: a dead man being carried off to Hades

CHARON: the ferry man transporting the dead to Hades

CHORUS OF FROGS

CHORUS OF INITIATES: worshippers of the gods of the 
underworld

AEACUS: a gatekeeper in Hades

SERVANT

FIRST HOSTESS (PANDOKEUTRIA)

SECOND HOSTESS (PLATANE)

SERVANT OF PLUTO

EURIPIDES: the playwright

AESCHYLUS: the playwright

PLUTO: king of Hades

VARIOUS ATTENDANTS

 

[The play opens on a street leading to Hades, with a 
door in the centre of the backstage area. Enter Dionysus, appearing as a 
middle-aged man with a noticeable paunch, wearing a yellow tunic and over that a 
lion skin. Heâs carrying a huge club, one commonly associated with Hercules. On 
his feet he wears soft leather lace-up boots. Behind him comes his slave 
Xanthias riding on a donkey and carrying a huge amount of luggage. Xanthias 
notices the audience]

 

XANTHIAS

Look, master, an audience! 
Shouldnât I say something?

Tell them one of those jokes they always fall for?

 

DIONYSUS

O, all rightâsay what you like. 
Only no jokes

about how youâre dying to piss. I canât stand thoseâ

theyâre all so stale.

 

XANTHIAS

                              
What about my other jokes?

 

DIONYSUS

Go aheadâjust nothing about 
your bladder,

about how itâs going to burst.

 

XANTHIAS

                                       
What? You mean I canât tell

that really funny one . . .

 

DIONYSUS

                                     
I suppose soâ

but donât say anything about the bit.

 

XANTHIAS

 

                                               
What bit?

 

DIONYSUS

The bit about how you need to 
shift your load                              

10

to take a piss.

 

XANTHIA

                               
Not even this oneâ

âHere I am transporting such a load

if I get no relief I may explode.â                                                             

 [10]

 

DIONYSUS

Please, please, don't talk about that 
oneâ

not unless Iâm sick and need to throw up.

 

XANTHIAS

Then whatâs the point of my 
being here like this?

Why do I get to carry all the heavy baggage

if I canât tell the usual porter jokesâyou know,

the ones Ameipsias and Phrynichus

and Lycias, too, in all their comedies
                                     
 

        

  20

provide the slave who carries all the bags?
(1)

 

DIONYSUS

Just donât. Those jokes are all 
so feebleâ

when I have to watch a play and hear them

by the time I leave Iâve aged at least a year.

 

XANTHIAS 

[striking a heroic tragic pose]

Alas, for my neck beneath this 
triply damned yoke.

I suffer all this pressure and canât tell my joke.                                    

  [20]

 

DIONYSUS

Itâs an outrage, sheer 
insolence, that I,

Dionysus, son of Winejar, have to walk like this,

sweating along so he can ride at ease

without a care and carrying no load.

 

XANTHIAS

                                                 
What!?                                             

 30

Arenât I carrying the load?

 

DIONYSUS

                              
How can you be?

Youâre riding on your ass.

 

XANTHIAS

                                
Iâm loaded down.

All this stuff . . .

 

DIONYSUS

                         
What do you mean by that?

 

XANTHIAS

What I just said carries lots of weight.

 

DIONYSUS

Isnât the donkey carrying our load?

 

XANTHIAS

No, no way. Not the load Iâm holding.

 

DIONYSUS

                                                    
How come?

How can you be carrying anything at all

when someone else is carrying you?

 

XANTHIAS

                                             
Iâve no idea.

But my shoulderâs falling off.                                                                  

[30]

 

DIONYSUS

                                                   
All right, then.

Since you claim the donkeyâs useless to you,                                 

  40

why not take your turn and carry it?

 

XANTHIAS

                               
What a wretched life!

I should have gone away to fight at seaâ

then Iâd be free and Iâd have told you 
 

straight

what you could do with that ass of yours.
(2)

 

DIONYSUS

Get down, you useless idiot! 
Weâre thereâ

by the door Iâm aiming for, my first stop.

 

[Dionysus knocks very aggressively on the door and 
calls out in a very imperious tone.]

 

Hey, in there! Doorman! Iâm summoning you.

 

[The door opens and Hercules steps out, wearing a 
lionâs skin and carrying a club. Heâs amazed that someone is dressed up to 
resemble him.]

 

HERCULES

Whoâs banging on this 
doorâsmashing at it

like some wild centaur. My god, whatâs this?

 

[Hercules inspects Dionysusâ outfit and starts to 
laugh uproariously.]

 

DIONYSUS

Hey, my boy . . .

 

XANTHIAS

                        
What?

 

DIONYSUS

                                   
Didnât you see?

 

XANTHIAS

                                                              
See what?                           

  50
  
   [40]

 

DIONYSUS

How scared he was of me?

 

XANTHIAS

                                  
Yes, by god, he was,

scared youâre nuts.

 

HERCULES 

[doubling up with laughter]

                                             
By holy Demeter,

I canât stop laughing. Iâll try biting my lip.

No, no use. I canât stop laughing at him.

 

DIONYSUS

Come here, my good man. I need something from you.

 

HERCULES 

[still laughing out of control]

I canât help myselfâheâs so 
ridiculous.

Seeing that lion skin above that yellow dress.

Whatâs going on? Do people with large clubs

now walk around in leather booties? 

Where on earth do you think youâre going?                                   

 60

 

DIONYSUS

Iâve done naval service under Cleisthenes.
(3)

 

HERCULES

At that sea battle?

 

DIONYSUS

                          
Yesâand sunk enemy ships,

twelve or thirteen of them.                                                                  

      [50]

 

HERCULES

                                  
Just the two of you?

 

DIONYSUS

Yes, by Apollo, we did.

 

XANTHIAS

                                   
Then I woke up.

 

DIONYSUS

I was on board with Euripides
â

Andromeda
,

reading to myself aloud, when suddenly

a huge urge seized my heart. Youâve no idea how 
strong.

 

HERCULES

An urge? How big was it?

 

DIONYSUS

                                   
The size of Molonâtiny.
(4)

 

HERCULES

For a woman?

 

DIONYSUS

                     
No, no.

 

HERCULES

                                  
A young lad, then? 

 

DIONYSUS

Certainly not.

 

HERCULES

                     
Well, then, a man? 

 

DIONYSUS

                                                      
Ugh!                                           

  70

 

HERCULES

Did you grab hold of your Cleisthenes?

 

DIONYSUS

Donât mock me, brother.
(5)
 Iâm 
not doing so well,

tormented by such hot desires.

 

HERCULES

                                             
Tell me,

my little brother, whatâs it like?

 

DIONYSUS

                                     
I canât explain.                                                   

 [60]

But Iâll try to show you by analogy.

Have you ever had a craving for some stew?
(6)

 

HERCULES

For stew? In my life maybe ten thousand times.

 

DIONYSUS

Is that explanation clear 
enough to you?

Or shall I try some other way?

 

HERCULES

                             
Not about stew! 

That I understand completely. 

 

DIONYSUS

                                                               
Well then,                         

  80

thatâs how much Iâm eaten up with my desire

for Euripides.

 

HERCULES

                         
Even when heâs dead?
(7)

 

DIONYSUS

So no oneâs going to talk me 
out of itâ

I have to find him.

 

HERCULES

                        
Right down in Hell?

 

DIONYSUS

                                                   
Or even lower,

by god, if thereâs such a place.                                                              

  [70]

 

HERCULES

                                      
Whatâs the point of that?

 

DIONYSUS

I need a clever poet. Thereâs 
none around.

The ones weâve got are all so wretched.

 

HERCULES

What? Isnât Iophon still up there?
(8)

 

DIONYSUS

Heâs the only good one leftâif 
heâs any good.

Iâm not really sure if thatâs the case.                                               

  90

 

HERCULES

If youâve got to take a 
playwright back,

why not Sophocles? Heâs better than Euripides.

 

DIONYSUS

Not âtil I get Iophon all by 
himself,

without his father, Sophocles, so I can test

the metal of his poetry. Besides, Euripides

is such a rascal he may try to flee Hades                                              

   [80]

and come with me. But Sophocles was niceâ

easygoing while on earth and down there, too.

 

HERCULES

What about Agathon? Whereâs he? 

 

DIONYSUS

                                                 
Heâs left usâ 

a fine poet lamented by his friends.                                                

 100

 

HERCULES

Whereâs he gone?

 

DIONYSUS

                            
Off to feast with saints.
(9)

 

HERCULES

And Xenocles?

 

DIONYSUS

                      
O by god, may he drop dead!

 

HERCULES

Well then, Pythangelos?
(10)

 

XANTHIAS

                                                        
What about me
?

In pain all this timeâmy shoulder's sore as hell.

 

HERCULES

Surely you have other 
artsy-fartsy typesâ

thousands of tragic poetsâall of them                                                

    [90]

way more wordy than Euripides?

 

DIONYSUS

                                                                             
No, noâ

all chatterboxes, twittering swallows in a music hall,

mere foliageâdisgraces to the artistâs craft. 

Once they get a chance to stage their plays,                                 

   110

to crap all over tragedy, they disappear.

If you looked youâd never find one playwright,

someone creative who could well declaim

a worthy sentiment.

 

HERCULES

                                
That word âcreativeââ

whatâs it mean?

 

DIONYSUS

                         
Someone poetical enough

to give utterance to something grand,

something like

 

[Dionysus strikes a tragic pose.]

 

                                                 
âthe sky, Zeusâs pied-a-terre,â

âthe foot of time,â or thisââa mind that will not 
swear                       

  [100]

on sacred offerings but a perjured tongue 

thatâs false with no sense of its perfidy.â                                        

  120

 

HERCULES

You like that stuff?

 

DIONYSUS

                           
Like it? Iâm crazy about it.

 

HERCULES

I swear itâs all bullshitâand you know it.

 

DIONYSUS

Now, now, donât try to tell me 
what to think,

not with tragedy. Youâre no expert there.

 

HERCULES

I still say it sounds like total rubbish.

 

DIONYSUS

Why not teach me how to stuff my guts?

 

XANTHIAS

 WHAT ABOUT ME??!!!!!

 

DIONYSUS

                      Thatâs the reason Iâve come here

and dressed like youâso you can fill me in,

in case I need to know, about this placeâ 

who welcomed you down here, who'd 
 
you meet                  
 

          

 130
  
  [110]

that time you went down after Cerberus.
(11)

Tell me about the harbours, resting places,

bakeries and brothels, water fountains,

the cities, highways, all the detours,

the local customs and the fine hotels,

the ones with fewest bugs.

 

XANTHIAS

                                     Still no word of me.

 

HERCULES

O you valiant heart! Are you man enough

to venture down below?

 

DIONYSUS

                                                    Forget my courage.

Show me the highway, the shortest one there is, 

that takes me directly down to Hades.                                           

 140

Donât prattle on about the temperatureâ

and say it's way too hot or cold for me.

 

HERCULES

Letâs see . . . what should I mention first of all?                                    

  [120]

Which one? Hmmm. You could try a stool and ropeâ

you could just hang yourself.

 

DIONYSUS

                                   Stop it right there.

That way gives me a choking feeling.

 

HERCULES

Thereâs a straight short cut, well traveled, tooâ

with pestle and mortar . . .

 

DIONYSUS

                   
You mean hemlock.
(12)

 

HERCULES

                                                    Thatâs it!

 

DIONYSUS

Too coldâtoo much like winter. Right away 

the shins get frozen solid.

 

HERCULES

                                                         All right, then.                         

150

You want me to tell you how to get there fast.

 

DIONYSUS

Yes, by god. Iâm not one to take a hike.

 

HERCULES

How about a stroll to Kerameikos . . . 
(13)

 

DIONYSUS

Okay, what then?

 

HERCULES                       

                               Climb up the tower thereâ

right to the very top . . .

 

DIONYSUS

                             And then what?                                                        
    [130]

 

HERCULES

Take a look at the torch race starting upâ

when the spectators all yell out âTheyâre off!â

then off you go as well.

 

DIONYSUS

                               Off? Where to?

 

HERCULES

                                                               Down.

 

DIONYSUS

No, I canât take that road. Iâd pulverize 

both rissole wrappers of my brain.

 

HERCULES

                                                  Whatâs left?                                    
   160

 

DIONYSUS

The road you used.

 

HERCULES

                               O, an enormous journey!

At the very start you come to a vast lakeâ

immense and bottomless.

 

DIONYSUS

                                      How do I get across?

 

HERCULES

In a tiny boatâminisculeâlike this 

[indicating the 
size]
.

An ancient sailor takes you for a feeâ

two obols.                                                                                               

   [140]

DIONYSUS

                        Two obols? Itâs
 amazing

what two obols can buy anywhere.
(14)

How come itâs here in Hades, too?

 

HERCULES

                                                       That was Theseus.
(15)

He started it. Once past the lake youâll find snakes.

Youâll see thousands of them, horrific monsters.                           

   170

 

DIONYSUS

Donât keep trying to scare me. That wonât work.

Thereâs no way youâll get me to turn back.

 

HERCULES

Then a huge sewer, always full of liquid turdsâ

and lying in it anyone who harmed a guest

or screwed a lad and then took back the cash,

or smacked his mother, punched his fatherâs jaw,

or swore false oaths, 
 
or else had copied out                                       
 

  

   [150]

a speech of Morsimus.
(16)

 

DIONYSUS

                                            By god, with them in the 

shit

should lie whoever learned a war dance by Cinesias.
(17)
 

 

HERCULES

Next the breath of flutes will sound around you.                          

   180

Youâll see the finest light, just like in Athens,

and myrtle groves, with happy men and women

gathered there to celebrate and clap their hands.

 

DIONYSUS

So who are they?

 

HERCULES

                                Those are
 the initiates,

the ones who celebrate the mysteries.
(18)

 

XANTHIAS

Then, by god, in these mysteries I play the ass.

Iâll not stand for this a moment longer.                                                

   [160]

 

[Xanthias dismounts and starts to unload the baggage 
he has been carrying.]

 

HERCULES

Those ones will tell you all you need to know.

These initiates live closest to the road 
 

 

which takes you to the doors of Plutoâs place.
(19)
                          

    190

And so, my brother, I bid you fond farewell.

 

DIONYSUS

Good byeâgod keep you healthy, too.

 

[Hercules exits back through the door. Dionysus turns 
to Xanthias, who has just about finished putting down all the luggage he has 
been carrying.]

 

You thereâtake up the baggage once again!

 

XANTHIAS

Before Iâve put it down?

 

DIONYSUS

                                      Yes, and hurry up.

 

[Enter a solemn funeral cortege parrying a dead man 
towards Hades.]

 

XANTHIAS

Come on, Iâm begging you. Hire one of themâ

someone carrying the corpse. Thatâs why theyâre here.

 

DIONYSUS

And if I donât find anyone?

 

XANTHIAS

                                                 Iâll do it.

 

DIONYSUS

Fair enough. All right, theyâre bringing out a corpse                           

    [170]

You there . . . you stiff . . . Iâm talking to you . . 
. Hallo! 

 

[The corpse suddenly sits up straight.]

 

You want to take a little luggage down to hell?                            
   200

 

CORPSE

How much?

 

DIONYSUS

                  This stuff here.

 

CORPSE

                                   Will you pay two drachmas?

 

DIONYSUS

My god, no. Less than that.

 

CORPSE

                                         Then go away.

 

DIONYSUS

Hang on, my dear fellow. Canât we haggle?

 

CORPSE

If you donât pay two drachmas, forget it.

 

DIONYSUS

How about nine obols?

 

CORPSE

                                                   No bloody way!

Iâd rather you shoved me back to life again.

 

[Corpse lies down and the funeral procession moves 
away.]

 

DIONYSUS

What a pompous boor!

 

XANTHIAS

                                       To hell with himâ

Iâll take the stuff myself.

 

[Xanthias starts loading himself with the baggage once 
again.]

 

DIONYSUS

                                                   Thatâs my good manâ

a loyal and worthy slave. Letâs get that boat . . . .

 

[Enter Charon rowing his small boat across the stage.]

 

CHARON

Ahoy there! Coming alongside.                                                             
  [180]

 

XANTHIAS

                                       Whatâs this?

 

DIONYSUS

                                                                  This?                               

  210

By god, itâs the lake Hercules talked about.

And I see the boat . . .

 

XANTHIAS

                   Youâre right. Thanks to Poseidon.

This must be Charon.

 

DIONYSUS

                                      Ahoy there, Charon . . .

Greetings, Charon . . . Charon, halloooo!

 

CHARON

Whoâs seeks a rest from work and trouble?

Whoâs heading for Fields of Forgetfulness,

Never-never land, the 
 
Cerberians,

the Ravens and Tartarus?
(20)

 

DIONYSUS

                                  Thatâs me.

 

CHARON

Then jump aboard.       

 

DIONYSUS

                            Where do you put in? 

The Ravens? Is that a stop?

 

CHARON

                                         Yes, by godâ                                          

   220

a special stop just for you. Get in.

 

DIONYSUS 
[to Xanthias]

All right, my lad, hop in.

 

CHARON

                                        I wonât take the slaveâ                                
     [190]

not unless he fought at sea to save his skin.

 

XANTHIAS

Not me, by god, no way. My eyes were bad.

 

CHARON

Then you must make a detour round the lake.

 

XANTHIAS

Where do I wait for you?

 

CHARON

                                        At
 Wuthering Rockâ

right by the rest stop.
(21)

 

DIONYSUS

                             You got that?

 

XANTHIAS

                                                      I got that.

 

[picking up the bags]

 

Why am I so unlucky? When we began

I must've really pissed somebody off. 

 

CHARON 
[to Dionysus]

Sit down thereâat that oar. 

 

[Dionysus sits on one of the oars.]

 

                                                        Anyone else?                             

  230

Hurry upâall aboard! What are you doing?

 

DIONYSUS

What am I doing? Iâm sitting on this oar.

Thatâs what you ordered me to do.

 

CHARON

Come on, fatsoâpark your butt right here.

 

DIONYSUS 
[moving off the oar]

                                                     There!                                                 
  [200]

 

CHARON

Can you pick up the oar? Stretch your arms.

 

DIONYSUS

                                                        Like this?

 

CHARON

Donât be such a fool. Set your foot there.

Now pull the oar with all your force.

 

DIONYSUS

                                          How can I?

Iâve had no practice. Iâm no sailor.

And besides, Iâm not from Salamis.
(22)
 

How am I supposed to row a boat?                                               

     240

 

CHARON

Itâs not hard. Youâll hear lovely melodies

once you make the effort.

 

DIONYSUS

                            Songs? Whose songs?

 

CHARON

The amazing music of the swan frogs.

 

DIONYSUS

All right, then. Get the tempo going.

 

CHARON

Yo ho, heave ho. Yo ho heave ho.

 

[As the small boat begins to move, the Chorus of Frogs 
is heard from off stage.]
(23)

 

CHORUS OF FROGS 

Brekekekex koax koax

Brekekekex koax koax.                                                                           

   [210]

Children of the marsh and lake

harmonious song now sweetly make, 

our own enchanting melodies                                                        

    250

koax koax.

The songs we sang for Nysaâs lord,

for Dionysus, son of Zeus,

in Limnai at the Feast of Jars

as people in their drunken 
 
glee

thronged into our sanctuary.
(24)

Brekekekex koax koax.                                                                            

 [220]

 

DIOYSUS 
[still rowing]

Iâm starting to get a pain in the ass

from all your koax koax. 

 

CHORUS OF FROGS

Brekekekex koax koax.                                                                   
    260

 

DIONYSUS

Not that you give a damn about it.

 

CHORUS OF FROGS

Brekekekex koax koax.

 

DIONYSUS

Piss offâand take that koax koax with you.

Nothing but koax koax.

 

CHORUS OF FROGS

Yes, and for us thatâs fine

you meddling foolâso asinine.
